title: Spiral constants of shells give no valid evidence of ancestry

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Spiral constants of shells give no valid evidence of ancestry

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The constant angle of a shell's spiral, like its size, is no evidence of which form is more primitive or ancestral, nor does an intermediate angle show that a shell is intermediate in time or descent; phylogenetic series built from straight, loosely coiled and closely coiled cephalopod shells are not supported by the mathematical study of shell form.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: _To such phylogenetic hypotheses the mathematical or dynamical study of the forms of shells lends no valid support._ If we have two shells in which the constant angle of the spire be respectively 80° and 60°, that fact in itself does not at all justify an assertion that the one is more primitive, more ancient, or more “ancestral” than the other.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter XI, “The Logarithmic Spiral”; topic “Spiral form and phylogeny”. Scope: cephalopod (nautiloid and ammonoid) shell forms and phylogenetic inference from them

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch11-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.65

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Existing fossil and morphology data can quantify how informative spiral angle is about age and descent. They cannot prove that angle provides no evidence in every model, but can resolve the historical series and convergence components.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Using independently inferred cephalopod phylogenies and stratigraphy, test whether spiral angle alone predicts ancestor-descendant order or primitiveness after accounting for size and clade. Frequent convergence and poor temporal prediction would support the warning against inference from angle alone.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Independent fossil phylogenies remain uncertain.

The phrase 'no valid evidence' is methodological rather than a simple empirical frequency claim.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Living molluscs have trees that do not depend on shell angle, and shell scans can supply the angles, so a restricted test is possible. Fossil series from straight to coiled shells are the historically important case, and there the phylogeny is morphology-heavy. The analysis can show whether angle tracks ancestry in living groups and cannot cleanly vindicate or dismiss the fossil phylogenetic series Thompson rejects.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare spiral angle with phylogenetic distance or ancestral states estimated without using coiling as a character. If angle does not predict which form is ancestral or intermediate, the claim that it is not evidence of ancestry is supported; a robust phylogenetic signal would refute that denial.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
No evidence of ancestry is an epistemic claim: a weak correlation need not count as valid support, and the threshold is a judgement.

Ammonoid cladograms have often used coiling, so a fossil test can become circular.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:

discriminating power: 0.45
data existence: 0.65
analysis feasibility: 0.55
data adequacy: 0.5
